title: Start an Agent Session in GCP
subtitle: Advanced · Claude Code and OpenCode

scenes.title: Place the terminal in GCP
scenes.body: This walkthrough uses a simulated corporate workspace and a synthetic training repository.
scenes.code:
Corporate GCP workspace
├── Claude Code
├── OpenCode
└── training-orders checkout
scenes.result: Lab data · synthetic
scenes.narration: Start by locating the workspace where the coding agent is allowed to operate. In this course, Claude Code and OpenCode run inside the corporate Google Cloud workspace. The terminal and repository shown here are synthetic training examples. Keep your session inside the approved remote workspace. We will verify the environment before we give either agent a task.

scenes.title: Check the working directory
scenes.body: Use read-only checks to identify the checkout and its starting state.
scenes.code:
pwd
git status --short --branch
git rev-parse --short HEAD
scenes.result:
/work/training-orders
## lab/a01
27e4ab1
scenes.narration: In the approved terminal, check the current directory, branch, and short commit identifier. These small checks tell you which checkout the agent can see and where to find your starting point later. The example is clean on a lab branch. If your actual checkout contains someone else's work, leave it in place and switch to an approved training checkout.

scenes.title: Identify the installed clients
scenes.body: Keep the tool and the installed version in your lab notes.
scenes.code:
claude --version
opencode --version
scenes.result: Record the versions shown by your workspace.
scenes.narration: Now check the versions of Claude Code and OpenCode that the organization has installed. Features, selectors, and available controls can change across versions. For that reason, the lab records what the terminal actually reports. A missing command is an access or setup question for the workspace owner. Use the client your organization provides for this exercise.

scenes.title: Record the resolved model
scenes.body: Distinguish the client, selected model, and configured provider.
scenes.code:
Client       Claude Code or OpenCode
Model        Value shown in the session
Provider     Workspace configuration
Location     Approved GCP workspace
scenes.result: Capture display names or IDs. Leave secrets out.
scenes.narration: Inspect the model selection in the authorized client. Record the exact model identifier if it is available, along with the configured provider. The program that runs on the workstation, the model that interprets the task, and the service that processes the request are separate parts of the session. The workspace administrator can confirm any setting that your account cannot see.

scenes.title: Confirm what the session may do
scenes.body: Read the effective policy before asking for edits or commands.
scenes.code:
Read training repository     Allowed
Edit lab branch              Ask first
Run approved unit tests      Ask first
External integrations        Closed
scenes.result: Illustrative policy. Verify the real settings.
scenes.narration: This example gives the agent access to read the training repository and asks for confirmation before editing or running its tests. Other workspaces may apply a different policy. Check the effective rules in the client and the surrounding environment. Keep project guidance, tool permission, and the runtime boundary separate when you reason about what the agent can do.

scenes.title: Begin with a read-only task
scenes.body: Ask the agent to trace a small path you can verify by opening the files.
scenes.code:
Locate the quantity validator and its unit tests.
Return the file paths and the test case for zero.
Use read-only inspection for this request.
scenes.result:
orders/quantity.py
 tests/test_quantity.py
scenes.narration: Start with a small inspection. Ask the agent to find the quantity validator and the associated unit tests, then give you their file paths. This is a useful first task because you can open each file to verify the result. If the client proposes an edit or command outside the stated scope, pause and inspect the request before approving it.

scenes.title: Verify the paths and starting state
scenes.body: Review the evidence directly and confirm that no edits were made.
scenes.code:
git status --short --branch
sed -n '1,24p' orders/quantity.py
scenes.result:
## lab/a01
Read the function and compare its path.
scenes.narration: Open the cited file yourself and confirm that it contains the relevant function. Then run the status check again. In this inspection, the working tree should look exactly as it did at the start. This final check gives you something concrete to compare with the agent's summary, and it reinforces a habit we will use before every handoff.

scenes.title: Save a short session record
scenes.body: Carry this information into the next Advanced lab.
scenes.code:
Workspace  →  branch  →  commit
Client     →  model   →  provider
Scope      →  tools   →  result
scenes.result: Ready for the versioned-instructions lab.
scenes.narration: Before ending, write down the workspace, branch, starting commit, client version, model, and permission scope. Keep the record concise. You now have an auditable description of the environment and a verified read-only result. In the next lab, that description will help you compare how the two clients discover instructions and skills from the same repository.

title: Version Instructions and Skills Across Tools
subtitle: Advanced · One repository, two agent clients

scenes.title: Start with a convention you can test
scenes.body: Both GCP clients will work on the same synthetic training checkout.
scenes.code:
Lab convention
Run the quantity test suite after a validator change.
Report the command, outcome, and checked files.
scenes.result: A reviewer can verify all three items.
scenes.narration: We will share a simple engineering convention across Claude Code and OpenCode in the approved Google Cloud workspace. After a change to the validator, the workflow calls for a focused test and a short evidence summary. Choose a convention you can check from the result. That gives you a practical way to verify that the guidance reached the session.

scenes.title: Place persistent guidance in the repository
scenes.body: Use the supported project-level instruction files for each client and version.
scenes.code:
CLAUDE.md
AGENTS.md

Tests: python -m unittest discover -s tests -v
scenes.result: Same convention. Confirm both load paths.
scenes.narration: Project instructions carry conventions that apply to work in the repository. In this example, the repository contains the instruction file used by each configured client. Some versions and configurations support shared instructions or imports. Check the documentation and what your session actually loads. Keep the convention short enough that a teammate can review it easily.

scenes.title: Put the procedure in a skill
scenes.body: Give the agent a reusable method for producing a test evidence summary.
scenes.code:
---
name: training-test-evidence
description: Summarize test evidence for training PRs.
---
Record command, outcome, and inspected files.
scenes.result: SKILL.md · focused and versioned
scenes.narration: A skill gives the agent a reusable procedure for a particular job. Write a clear description, so the client can decide when the procedure is relevant, and include the steps and output format in the body of the skill. This example contains a test evidence procedure. Keep supporting templates with the skill when the selected client supports that layout.

scenes.title: Verify each configured discovery path
scenes.body: The two clients can discover skills in different locations.
scenes.code:
Example project-relative locations
.claude/skills/training-test-evidence/SKILL.md
.opencode/skills/training-test-evidence/SKILL.md
scenes.result: Verify version, location, and precedence.
scenes.narration: The same skill can be placed where each client is configured to discover it. Confirm the paths and precedence for the installed versions, especially if the workspace provides managed policies or additional skill directories. If you maintain two files, keep their contents aligned and review changes together. Treat discovery as something to verify, rather than inferring it from a filename.

scenes.title: Check the skill on a relevant task
scenes.body: Use a recorded, synthetic test run as the input.
scenes.code:
Summarize the supplied validation evidence.
Produce the training PR evidence summary.
scenes.result:
Command · python -m unittest discover -s tests
Outcome · 4 passed
Scope · quantity validator and boundary test
scenes.narration: Start a fresh authorized session in each client. Give both sessions the same recorded test results and ask for the training pull request evidence summary. Check that the returned text includes the command, the outcome, and the files that were inspected. When the client shows a skill invocation, capture that signal as well. Confirm the result against the input.

scenes.title: Try an unrelated request
scenes.body: Check that the procedure does not dominate other tasks.
scenes.code:
Explain how order IDs are formatted.
Cite the source file.
scenes.result: Expected: an explanation with a source path.
scenes.narration: Run an unrelated request about order identifiers. The evidence summary procedure should be irrelevant here, although the repository's general guidance may still apply. Look for evidence in the response and any invocation record. This pairing of one matching request and one unrelated request is a small behavior check you can repeat when the description or installed version changes.

scenes.title: Confirm the tool boundary
scenes.body: Use the workspace policy to decide which actions can run.
scenes.code:
Instruction: report the test command
Skill: format the evidence
Permission: authorize the command separately
scenes.result: Human review remains part of the PR.
scenes.narration: A repository instruction or skill can describe what an agent should do. The host and workspace determine what it is allowed to do. If a test command requires approval, read and approve the exact command only in the authorized environment. The training reviewer still checks the final result and records any pull request decision using their own account.

scenes.title: Review the instructions as code
scenes.body: Keep guidance and its verification together in a small diff.
scenes.code:
git diff -- CLAUDE.md AGENTS.md
Expected evidence fields
- command
- outcome
- scope
scenes.result: Compare results in Claude Code and OpenCode.
scenes.narration: Review and version the files through the repository's ordinary human review process. Include the exact versions and the outcomes of your matching and unrelated tasks in the evidence. A teammate should be able to reproduce the behavior and see why the instructions belong in the project. The next lab applies these conventions to a change across several files.

title: Run a Multi-File Change in Stages
subtitle: Advanced · Scoped implementation in GCP

sources.label: DORA on working in small batches

scenes.title: Set a narrow goal
scenes.body: This simulated refactor centralizes a quantity rule while preserving behavior.
scenes.code:
Issue #31 · Centralize the order quantity rule
Accept a positive integer.
Reject zero and negative values.
Keep command and API outputs the same.
scenes.result: Approved scope: rule, two callers, tests.
scenes.narration: For this lab, two paths in the synthetic repository each validate an order quantity. The issue asks us to centralize that rule while preserving both existing interfaces. Before opening the approved agent session in GCP, identify the parts of this work that are in scope. Our boundary is the shared rule, two callers, and their existing tests.

scenes.title: Record the behavior before editing
scenes.body: Check the clean branch and run the approved focused suite.
scenes.code:
git status --short --branch
python -m unittest discover -s tests -v
scenes.result: Example baseline: 8 tests passed.
scenes.narration: Begin with a clean training branch and run the existing tests in the authorized environment. Confirm that both callers have a positive case and a zero or negative case. Save the result with the starting commit. A known baseline gives you a concrete way to detect an unintended change once the agent begins editing.

scenes.title: Ask for one stage at a time
scenes.body: Give the agent the issue, call sites, and validation command.
scenes.code:
Stage 1: extract the shared rule and migrate the CLI.
Stage 2: migrate the API caller.
Run the relevant tests after each stage.
Wait for my review before starting the next stage.
scenes.result: Two reviewable diffs instead of one broad edit.
scenes.narration: In an approved agent client, ask for a plan with an explicit stop after each stage. Have the agent identify the actual call sites and the tests it will run. Open the referenced files and check that the plan fits the issue. Once you approve the first stage, keep the second stage pending until the first stage is verified.

scenes.title: Inspect the first implementation
scenes.body: Check the new shared rule and the one caller in scope.
scenes.code:
git diff --stat
git diff -- orders/quantity.py orders/cli.py
scenes.result:
Shared function extracted.
CLI now calls the shared function.
scenes.narration: After the first stage, review the diff in the affected files. Look at the comparison itself, the public behavior of the command, and the tests that demonstrate compatibility. If the agent proposes the focused test command, confirm that it is the approved command for this checkout. Keep the proof from this run before asking it to proceed.

scenes.title: Pause a change outside the issue
scenes.body: Review the work proposed for the second caller before it runs.
scenes.code:
Proposed edit
orders/api.py           In scope
infra/deploy.yaml       Outside scope
scenes.result: Decision: keep the API edit; omit infrastructure.
scenes.narration: During the second stage, the example agent proposes touching a deployment file. The issue needs an API caller change and a check of its behavior. Pause before accepting the proposed edit. Point the agent at the approved files again and ask for a revised plan. Record the decision so the reviewer can see why the change stayed small.

scenes.title: Recheck the whole change
scenes.body: Run the same suite with both callers wired to the shared rule.
scenes.code:
git diff --name-only
python -m unittest discover -s tests -v
scenes.result:
orders/quantity.py · orders/cli.py · orders/api.py
Example result: 8 tests passed.
scenes.narration: When the second diff is ready, check the list of changed files as well as the actual changes. Run the same baseline suite, and confirm the original cases still hold for both callers. Make sure the test result belongs to the current revision. A pass from an earlier stage only proves the code that existed at that stage.

scenes.title: Turn the checkpoints into review evidence
scenes.body: A human author can prepare the PR after reviewing the final diff.
scenes.code:
Summary: shared quantity rule
Scope: CLI and API callers
Baseline: 8 passed
Final: 8 passed
Compatibility: public outputs preserved
scenes.result: Handoff to an independent human reviewer via gh.
scenes.narration: Summarize the behavior preserved, the code paths changed, and the baseline and final test results. Keep the final diff available for the author to review. The separate reviewer checks the pull request and its evidence from the approved terminal with GitHub CLI. This approach scales because each stage leaves evidence that another person can inspect.

scenes.title: Repeat the pattern on another small refactor
scenes.body: Choose two short stages and decide where human judgment matters.
scenes.code:
Baseline  →  Plan  →  Stage 1  →  Verify
                    Stage 2  →  Verify  →  PR
scenes.result: Each stage has one clear outcome.
scenes.narration: Try the same method on another training refactor. Pick an existing behavior, identify two short stages and give each stage a verification command. Notice which decisions the agent can make within the task and which decisions belong to a person. The most useful checkpoint is the one that catches a mistake while the diff is still small.

title: What Is MCP? Connect One Scoped Tool
subtitle: Advanced · An approved read-only integration

scenes.title: Trace the connection
scenes.body: The lab exposes one mock issue through a read-only training server.
scenes.code:
Agent client → MCP server → synthetic issue fixture
                         ↳ get_training_issue
scenes.result: One named tool, one defined read scope.
scenes.narration: Model Context Protocol, or M C P, is a way for a client to connect to servers that can supply tools and other context. Our simulated server exposes one tool that reads a synthetic training issue. We will follow the request from the approved GCP client, through the server, and back to the session where the result becomes evidence.

scenes.title: Verify the server and the available action
scenes.body: Review the approved integration before enabling it.
scenes.code:
Server       training-issues
Tool         get_training_issue
Data         synthetic orders issues only
Operation    read by issue number
scenes.result: Write operations are outside this lab scope.
scenes.narration: Begin with the workspace's approval record for the training server. Confirm its source, environment, and available tools. The operation here reads a single issue by number, in a synthetic project only. Confirm the actual access scope with the owner or supplied lab policy. A friendly tool name only helps you identify the action, so check the effective permissions as well.

scenes.title: Inspect the approved configuration
scenes.body: The demonstration shows the connection shape with fictitious settings.
scenes.code:
Training integration settings
server: training-issues
workspace: approved-lab
scope: read:synthetic-issues
scenes.result: Use managed settings from the workspace owner.
scenes.narration: Open the approved integration settings in Claude Code or OpenCode. Configuration fields and locations vary by client and version, so read what the workspace provides. Look for the configured identity and scope. If the integration is unavailable in the training workspace, follow along with the same input and recorded result supplied as a synthetic fixture.

scenes.title: Inspect the proposed tool call
scenes.body: Request one known practice issue and review the tool and argument.
scenes.code:
Fetch synthetic issue 17 and list its criteria.

get_training_issue({"issue_number":17})
scenes.result: Proposed read · tool name and input visible.
scenes.narration: Ask the agent for the acceptance criteria of issue seventeen. Before the call runs, inspect the proposed tool and its argument. Make sure the request points to the training issue. Follow the session's permission prompt if one appears. This is the point where you verify that the planned call matches both your intent and the approved data scope.

scenes.title: Trace the evidence into the answer
scenes.body: Read the returned data before accepting the agent's summary.
scenes.code:
Issue #17 · Reject zero order quantities
Positive integer quantities are accepted.
Zero and negative integers are rejected.
scenes.result: Agent output cites the synthetic issue record.
scenes.narration: Read the result returned from the training server. The issue provides two straightforward acceptance criteria. Check each item in the agent's summary against the response. The tool call supplies context for the model. Its text can describe the issue, but consequential actions still follow your instruction and the policy of the host.

scenes.title: Verify the write boundary from policy
scenes.body: Use the supplied permission record to inspect an out-of-scope action.
scenes.code:
Read issue 17         In scope
Post a PR comment     Outside scope
Change issue status   Outside scope
scenes.result: Keep the summary in the local training session.
scenes.narration: Look at the training permission record and check what happens when a proposed follow-up would write back to the repository. The scope only covers reads, so keep the summary in the session. In the engineering workflow, a person reviews the pull request using GitHub CLI. This keeps the source of evidence and the authorization to act easy to audit.

scenes.title: Save the smallest useful audit record
scenes.body: Retain the verified configuration details, tool input, and expected evidence.
scenes.code:
Server    training-issues
Action    get_training_issue(17)
Scope     read only
Evidence  two verified criteria
scenes.result: One successful read with an explicit boundary.
scenes.narration: Record the server name, the tool, the issue number, and what you verified from the response. Add the client version if discovery or approvals were central to this lab. You now have a small repeatable integration with a clear boundary. The next episode adds checks that can stop a workflow when its output misses an explicit requirement.

title: Design a Workflow with Deterministic Checks
subtitle: Advanced · Let evidence control the next step

scenes.title: Map the steps and the gates
scenes.body: Use the synthetic orders branch to show where judgment and repeatable checks belong.
scenes.code:
Issue → plan → regression → fix → diff → PR
         human   test exit code    human
scenes.result: The workflow carries evidence between steps.
scenes.narration: A workflow coordinates tasks, decisions, and checks in a defined order. In this synthetic example, the agent can choose how to inspect the quantity code and propose a small fix, while specific tests measure what the change does. Start by mapping the steps from issue to pull request. Mark where the workflow waits for a person or for an objective check.

scenes.title: Turn the requirement into observable outcomes
scenes.body: Use a known issue and write down the expected behavior for each example.
scenes.code:
Quantity    1     5     0     -1
Expected    yes   yes   no    no
scenes.result: Four cases illustrate the acceptance criteria.
scenes.narration: The training issue says that orders accept positive quantities. Put the four example cases into the test plan before asking for a code change. A deterministic unit test uses a fixed input and expected result, so you can repeat it after another edit. A short table also makes the requirement easier for a reviewer to evaluate.

scenes.title: Capture the failing case on the original code
scenes.body: Run the new regression test with the original implementation still in place.
scenes.code: python -m unittest discover -s tests -v
scenes.result:
test_rejects_zero ... FAIL
Expected rejection; observed acceptance.
scenes.narration: In the approved environment, add the regression test for zero and run it against the original implementation. The example fails with the expected assertion. Read the actual failure, because an import error or an unrelated assertion would not demonstrate this bug. Save the output and the source revision that produced it. Now the author can ask the agent for the minimal fix.

scenes.title: Define what happens after the test
scenes.body: Keep the acceptance test fixed while the implementation changes.
scenes.code:
Focused tests pass  → review diff
Focused tests fail  → inspect output
Unexpected files    → stop and inspect
scenes.result: A failed check prevents the review handoff.
scenes.narration: At this point, the workflow has one fixed gate. After the change, advance only when the required test command exits successfully and the diff fits the issue. A failure should lead to inspection of the output. Keep the regression test unchanged unless a person approves a correction to the test itself. This way the evidence stays comparable across attempts.

scenes.title: Run the same test command after the fix
scenes.body: Compare the new output with the earlier failure.
scenes.code:
git diff --stat
python -m unittest discover -s tests -v
scenes.result:
test_rejects_zero ... ok
4 tests passed.
scenes.narration: The example uses the same command after the code change. The regression now passes, and the previous cases still pass. Verify the exact revision and check the diff yourself. The passing run establishes the tested behavior. The human review still checks whether the source is clear, in scope, and appropriate for the repository.

scenes.title: Run independent checks on the PR
scenes.body: Use the repository's configured workflow and observe the current status.
scenes.code: gh pr checks 42
scenes.result:
Unit tests     pass
Format check   pass
scenes.narration: After the human author opens the training pull request, inspect its configured checks from the authorized terminal. Continuous integration should run the relevant tests for the proposed revision. Check names, elapsed time, and pending status belong to this repository's configuration. If a required check is pending or failed, wait for evidence or address the failure before proceeding.

scenes.title: Hand off evidence to the reviewer
scenes.body: Collect the required proof in the PR so another person can make the decision.
scenes.code:
Issue: #17
Regression: expected failure before the fix
Verification: four pass after the fix
Required checks: passed
scenes.result: Independent reviewer reads diff and records decision.
scenes.narration: Give the reviewer the issue, the test command, the failing and passing outcomes, and the final diff. The reviewer uses their own account and GitHub CLI to verify the details and record their decision. This workflow stays reliable because each step leads to a visible result, and the handoff depends on concrete evidence rather than an agent's claim.

title: RAG and Embeddings for Repository Knowledge
subtitle: Advanced · Retrieve evidence before answering

scenes.title: Start with a question the repository can answer
scenes.body: The exercise uses a small synthetic index of repository documentation.
scenes.code:
Question
Can an order have a quantity of zero?

Evidence should include a file and revision.
scenes.result: Goal: answer from the approved training repository.
scenes.narration: This exercise asks a simple question about repository policy. Can an order have a quantity of zero? We want an answer that points to the actual rule and the revision where it appears. The training index contains only synthetic repository documents. We will trace a retrieved passage into the answer, then check that passage directly.

scenes.title: Index small passages with useful metadata
scenes.body: Keep paths and revisions attached to each passage.
scenes.code:
docs/order-policy.md      rev 27e4ab1
  Quantity must be a positive integer.
docs/shipping-policy.md   rev 27e4ab1
  Delivery dates use the business calendar.
scenes.result: Each passage retains its source.
scenes.narration: Begin with a few short passages from approved files. Attach each file path and revision to the text. That metadata lets the reviewer check relevance and freshness after retrieval. Include a passage about shipping so the example has something nearby but unrelated. The size of the passage should preserve enough neighboring text to explain the rule accurately.

scenes.title: Represent passages for similarity search
scenes.body: An embedding is a numerical representation used to compare meaning.
scenes.code:
Passage text → embedding model → vector
Question     → embedding model → vector
Compare vectors for candidate passages.
scenes.result: Similarity helps find evidence. Open the source to verify.
scenes.narration: An embedding model maps text into a list of numbers that can be compared for similarity. In this example, the system embeds the question and the approved passages and compares their vectors. The point is to find useful candidate evidence. Similarity alone cannot confirm that a passage is current, applicable, or true, so keep the source metadata attached.

scenes.title: Inspect the passages selected for this question
scenes.body: This simulated retrieval chooses one relevant passage and one weak match.
scenes.code:
1  docs/order-policy.md@27e4ab1
   Quantity must be a positive integer.
2  docs/shipping-policy.md@27e4ab1
   Delivery dates use the business calendar.
scenes.result: Keep the order rule. Drop the unrelated passage.
scenes.narration: Look at the results before sending them onward. The first passage addresses the quantity rule and has a source path. The second passage discusses delivery dates, so it adds no evidence for this question. A useful retrieval step returns enough detail to support the answer and trims material that would distract the model or obscure the relevant source.

scenes.title: Ask for an answer grounded in the passage
scenes.body: Retrieval-augmented generation supplies the selected evidence with the question.
scenes.code:
Question: Can quantity be zero?
Evidence: docs/order-policy.md@27e4ab1
Rule: Quantity must be a positive integer.
Answer with the cited file and revision.
scenes.result: Zero is invalid. See docs/order-policy.md@27e4ab1.
scenes.narration: Now give the model the question and the selected passage. This combination is retrieval augmented generation, or R A G. Retrieval happens before the answer is generated. The response cites the order policy and applies the positive integer rule to zero. Open the cited file and confirm the answer against the exact text. The citation is evidence you can check.

scenes.title: Handle a stale or missing source
scenes.body: Ask the same question after withholding the relevant passage.
scenes.code:
Retrieved: shipping policy only
Question: can quantity be zero?
Evidence for the rule: unavailable
scenes.result: State that the supplied sources are insufficient.
scenes.narration: Now repeat the exercise with the order policy passage removed. The supplied material does not answer the quantity question. A good response identifies the missing evidence rather than guessing a rule. In a maintained repository, also check the revision and refresh the index when appropriate. These checks prevent an outdated or unrelated passage from becoming a confident answer.

scenes.title: Keep retrieval within the approved boundary
scenes.body: Use the same authorization rules for indexing and retrieving material.
scenes.code:
Index source: training repository only
Retrieve with authorized access
Keep path and revision in every result
Verify references against the checkout
scenes.result: Traceable evidence for each supported answer.
scenes.narration: Before adopting retrieval for an actual repository, confirm what may be indexed, where the index is stored, and which identities can retrieve it. In this course we illustrate the pattern with synthetic data. The same habit that helps a developer verify a code suggestion applies here. Record the evidence, confirm the source, and say when the available material is insufficient.

title: Evaluate Models and Agents on the Same Task
subtitle: Advanced · Compare behavior with a repeatable lab

scenes.title: Ask what you are trying to learn
scenes.body: This lab compares two complete agent configurations on a synthetic issue.
scenes.code:
Question
Which setup produces a smaller, reviewable fix?

Task: reject zero order quantities.
scenes.result: Compare complete setups on the same evidence.
scenes.narration: Before running a comparison, write down the practical question. Here we want to know which approved setup produces a small, reviewable fix for a synthetic defect. We will compare Claude Code and OpenCode inside the corporate GCP workspace. A result will describe the tested setup, the task, and the evidence that a reviewer can verify.

scenes.title: Use the same baseline for both runs
scenes.body: Prepare a fresh approved training checkout for each setup.
scenes.code:
git rev-parse --short HEAD
git status --short --branch
scenes.result:
Run A · 27e4ab1 · clean
Run B · 27e4ab1 · clean
scenes.narration: Start both sessions at the same commit and confirm that their checkouts are clean. Use separate training branches or equivalent isolated copies so the first run cannot influence the second. Give both configurations the same issue, source files, and acceptance criteria. Keep their test fixtures and your review rubric fixed throughout the comparison.

scenes.title: Write one prompt and record each setup
scenes.body: Record the model and provider along with the client and permissions.
scenes.code:
Task: fix zero quantity acceptance.
Scope: validator and regression test.
Evidence: diff plus test result.
Record: client, model, provider, permissions.
scenes.result: Both runs use the same task and test command.
scenes.narration: Use one task statement and give it to both sessions. For each run, record the exact model identifier, provider, client version, effective permissions, and context. If both setups can use the same model and settings, that can help focus the experiment on the client. If the models differ, treat the result as a comparison of complete configurations.

scenes.title: Decide what counts before seeing the result
scenes.body: Score correctness and scope before considering time.
scenes.code:
Required: regression and earlier tests pass
Required: only approved files changed
Record: human interventions
Record: time to verified handoff
scenes.result: Use the same rubric for both outcomes.
scenes.narration: Set the evaluation criteria before opening the output. First, the change needs to pass the independent tests and stay within scope. Then record how many times a person had to correct or redirect the session, and how much verification work remains. Start with measurements the reviewer can repeat, then add cost or response time if those affect your decision.

scenes.title: Capture evidence instead of trusting summaries
scenes.body: Inspect each diff and run the approved reference tests.
scenes.code:
git diff --name-only
git diff --stat
python -m unittest discover -s tests -v
scenes.result:
Run A: 4 passed · 2 files
Run B: 4 passed · 3 files
scenes.narration: For each completed run, look at the actual diff and run the same reference tests. The simulated results show both suites passing, with one run touching an extra file. Open that file and check it against the issue. Record why the edit does or does not belong to the task. A test pass and a clean scope check are separate pieces of evidence.

scenes.title: Compare the work a reviewer inherits
scenes.body: The numbers are synthetic examples used to illustrate the rubric.
scenes.code:
Run A   Run B
Tests passed              4       4
Outside-scope edits       0       1
Human redirects           1       2
Review time              4m      7m
scenes.result: Both pass tests. Run A meets the full scope rubric.
scenes.narration: Read the scorecard as a set of observations. In this synthetic example, both runs passed the tests. Run A stayed within scope and took less review time. Run B needed an extra redirect and inspection of another file. Record those observations separately, because they affect the human effort needed to reach a reviewable result.

scenes.title: Keep the conclusion tied to the experiment
scenes.body: Repeat with another task before choosing a default for the team.
scenes.code:
Keep: issue, prompt, commit, configuration
Save: diff, tests, interventions, review time
Repeat: another representative training task
scenes.result: Recommendations stay traceable to observed results.
scenes.narration: Write a conclusion that identifies the actual configurations, task, and evidence. This small comparison can tell you what to investigate next. Before recommending a default to the team, repeat it with representative tasks of different shapes and discuss the outcomes with reviewers. If measurements change across runs, report the range and use it to guide your next experiment.
